name: Person Swimming
baseMeaning: A picture of a swimmer in a cap and goggles, one arm extended forward in the water. Read in a message it lands as doing laps, going through the motions, staying afloat.
tldr: 🏊 Person Swimming. In a chat it comes across as doing laps, going through the motions, staying afloat.

contextMeanings.meaning: The plain reading: a swimmer in a cap and goggles, one arm extended forward in the water. Nothing hidden in the drawing itself.
contextMeanings.example: A weekly swim set done on autopilot 🏊

contextMeanings.meaning: Borrowed as a reaction, it reads as doing laps, going through the motions, staying afloat.
contextMeanings.example: Saying you are keeping your head above water 🏊

contextMeanings.meaning: In a dating thread the gesture is usually doing the work of a line that was not typed. It arrives as doing laps, going through the motions, staying afloat, softened by whatever sentence sits next to it.

In a work channel it is read the same way it is read anywhere else — doing laps, going through the motions, staying afloat — but the stakes of a misread are higher, because the sender is often talking about somebody's actual work.

platformNotes.note: In Slack 🏊 lands in channels where the sentence was supposed to be shorter. It is usually standing in for a weekly swim set done on autopilot, and a channel where the topic is somebody's workload is where it misreads.

On Discord 🏊 is a staple of the reaction bar, which is why it so often arrives stripped of its doing laps, going through the motions, staying afloat reading — a shape pressed rather than a message sent.

On X and Twitter 🏊 does most of its work in replies, where it tags a message like saying you are keeping your head above water. Short enough to survive being the whole post, which is exactly why it is used that way.

On iOS the Person Swimming 🏊 renders as the neutral drawing, and the neutral swatch is what most people send without thinking about it. A message like a weekly swim set done on autopilot is the kind that carries it — the picture lands before the sentence does.

WhatsApp renders 🏊 exactly as the phone system does, but the keyboard keeps it in the person-sport section, where nobody looks unless they are hunting for it. In family threads it tends to accompany a message like saying you are keeping your head above water.

generationalNotes.note: Gen Z reaches for 🏊 to do the work of a weekly swim set done on autopilot, and treats the neutral drawing as the default rather than as a choice. What they hear first is doing laps, going through the motions, staying afloat.

Millennials tend to send 🏊 deliberately, usually for something like saying you are keeping your head above water, and they read doing laps, going through the motions, staying afloat into it more often than the older cohorts do.
Gen X mostly uses 🏊 literally, as the picture of the gesture itself, and is less likely to read doing laps, going through the motions, staying afloat into it than younger senders are.
Older senders use 🏊 in the most straightforward way, on family and group messages, and are less likely to hear the doing laps, going through the motions, staying afloat subtext in it.

warnings.title: 🏊 and 🏄 get swapped
warnings.description: The Person Surfing 🏄 is one tap away in every picker, and it does not carry the same reading — the surfer rides a wave standing up, the swimmer is head-down in a pool doing laps. Check which one you actually picked.

warnings.title: The reading it usually gets is not the one it was sent with
warnings.description: People take 🏊 as something else fairly often: it gets read as a serious athlete or race effort when it is more often someone treading water through a slow week, since the cap and goggles look official. The sentence around it is usually what settles the meaning.

seoTitle: 🏊 Person Swimming Emoji - What It Actually Means in Text
seoDescription: 🏊 Person Swimming meaning: doing laps, going through the motions, staying afloat. How the emoji is used at work, at home and in dating threads, and where it goes wrong.

longForm.overview:
The drawing of 🏊 is a swimmer in a cap and goggles, one arm extended forward in the water. It arrived with Unicode 6.0 in the person-sport section, and in a conversation it does the work of a line somebody left out on purpose.

The line it stands in for is doing laps, going through the motions, staying afloat. That is the reading most people arrive with, and it is usually the intended one — a picture carries the same meaning as the sentence it replaces, and it arrives first.

The complication is that the drawing invites a second reading. It gets read as a serious athlete or race effort when it is more often someone treading water through a slow week, since the cap and goggles look official. In practice that second reading is not rare — it is the one that decides how a message lands, because the sender has usually not thought about it at all.

It also sits in the crowded part of the picker. The nearest neighbour is 🏄 Person Surfing: the surfer rides a wave standing up, the swimmer is head-down in a pool doing laps. The two are close enough that a fast thumb picks the wrong one, and the message goes out carrying a meaning nobody chose.

The person swimming also exists in five skin tones. They are separate pages with separate copy, because picking a tone is a decision in a way that picking the plain emoji is not: it says something about who the sender thinks the reader is.

In short — the person swimming reads as doing laps, going through the motions, staying afloat, it is most often used for a weekly swim set done on autopilot or saying you are keeping your head above water, and the five tone pages under it each say something different about who is sending it. The rest of the page takes those three apart.
longForm.howPeopleUseIt:
Context, not the picture, decides how this lands. 🏊 in a work thread is saying you are keeping your head above water; 🏊 in a family thread is a weekly swim set done on autopilot; 🏊 in a thread with somebody you like is a way of saying something you would rather not type out.

The tone versions of the emoji make the same point from the other side. The gesture is identical in all five, and the swatch says something about the sender before a word is read.

The shortest messages are the risky ones. A lone 🏊 is the whole reply, and it is carrying a meaning nobody wrote down — doing laps, going through the motions, staying afloat is the intention, but what arrives is a drawing. Everything the sentence would have disambiguated is simply missing.

Put it this way. A weekly swim set done on autopilot is the job the person swimming does most: it saves a sentence and lands faster than one would have. Saying you are keeping your head above water is the job it does second: there the picture is not the point, it is the temperature of the message.
longForm.whenNotToUse:
Think about what the emoji is replacing. If the sentence under it is doing the real work, 🏊 will get read as a serious athlete or race effort when it is more often someone treading water through a slow week, since the cap and goggles look official instead, and the thread ends up carrying a meaning nobody wrote.

And keep it away from first contact. There is nothing warm in the drawing, and a person swimming gesture used to answer other people's messages tends to sound like it is settling a point.

Keep it out of the formal register. In a thread about somebody's work, or in a message to somebody you have not met, 🏊 reads as doing laps, going through the motions, staying afloat, and formality is exactly where that reading does the most damage.

Leave 🏄 Person Surfing for the other message. The surfer rides a wave standing up, the swimmer is head-down in a pool doing laps. And keep 🏊 out of threads where somebody is hurting: it reads as doing laps, going through the motions, staying afloat there, because there is nothing in the drawing that says you meant well.
longForm.howToReply:
The safe move in an unclear thread is to answer the text. 🏊 gets read as a serious athlete or race effort when it is more often someone treading water through a slow week, since the cap and goggles look official often enough that the sentence matters more than the picture.

And do not send 🏊 alone when the message underneath is supposed to be warm. A message like a weekly swim set done on autopilot carries the feeling; the picture on its own leaves the reader choosing between doing laps, going through the motions, staying afloat and something sharper.

Start by reading what the 🏊 was doing. If it was a reaction, react: 🏊 back, and the thread is closed. If it was aimed at you, write. The difference matters, because the reply to a reaction can be a picture and the reply to a request cannot.

faqs.question: What is the difference between 🏊 and its skin-tone versions?
faqs.answer: The tone variants under person swimming show the same gesture in five different skin tones. The gesture does not change, but the tone is a small signal about who the sender imagines the reader is, and in some groups that signal is read louder than the sentence.

faqs.question: What does 🏊 mean in text?
faqs.answer: 🏊 is used for doing laps, going through the motions, staying afloat. The drawing shows a swimmer in a cap and goggles, one arm extended forward in the water, and that part is not in dispute — what changes is whether the sender is being literal or borrowing the gesture for a reaction.

faqs.question: What is the difference between 🏊 and 🏄?
faqs.answer: The surfer rides a wave standing up, the swimmer is head-down in a pool doing laps. The two sit close together in most pickers, so the difference is often about which one the sender pressed rather than about what they meant.

faqs.question: Is 🏊 rude?
faqs.answer: It can be. The gesture is meant as doing laps, going through the motions, staying afloat, but it gets read as a serious athlete or race effort when it is more often someone treading water through a slow week, since the cap and goggles look official. The risk is highest when it is the only message in the thread — a sentence gives the picture some context to sit in.

faqs.question: What does 🏊 mean from a guy?
faqs.answer: Nothing gender-specific. The same reading applies whoever sends it, and the meaning is set by the thread and by what is written next to it rather than by the sender.

conversationExamples.interpretation: A public sign-off, with the emoji as the full stop. The picture is doing the punctuation, which is why it is sent instead of a sentence.

conversationExamples.message: a weekly swim set done on autopilot 🏊
conversationExamples.interpretation: The everyday use: the picture carries the whole line. It lands as doing laps, going through the motions, staying afloat, and matching it with the same emoji is a normal reply.

conversationExamples.message: saying you are keeping your head above water 🏊
conversationExamples.interpretation: A handover or a sign-off in a channel. It reads as doing laps, going through the motions, staying afloat, and naming the next step in words is usually clearer than leaving it to the gesture.

conversationExamples.message: there is something you should know 🏊
conversationExamples.interpretation: A small joke or a nudge, with the emoji doing the tone work. It gets read as a serious athlete or race effort when it is more often someone treading water through a slow week, since the cap and goggles look official more easily here than it does in a work thread, because the thread is thinner.

conversationExamples.message: a weekly swim set done on autopilot 🏊
conversationExamples.interpretation: Family threads are where this lands most naturally. The reading is doing laps, going through the motions, staying afloat, and nobody in the thread is reading it as anything sharper than that.
